shots.narration: In November 1284, in the French city of Beauvais, part of the highest stone vaults of the Middle Ages came down. They stood more than 45 meters above the floor. The choir beneath them, the eastern arm of the cathedral, had been in use for just twelve years.
shots.visual_purpose: The real Beauvais filling the frame: the camera climbs the choir to its vault while 1284 is told, then pulls out to the choir seen from outside. The collapse is told, never shown [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)]

elements.text: Photo: Eusebius, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

shots.narration: And yet many buildings like it are still standing. At Amiens, begun in 1220, the vault rises more than 42 meters, in a building that is tall, slender and filled with light.
shots.visual_purpose: Amiens by its own photograph, filling the frame: the camera rises through the nave to its vault [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)]

elements.text: How did they raise stone that high?
And why, sometimes, did it come down?

shots.narration: The people who built them worked without modern structural calculations, relying on geometry, craft knowledge and experience. So how did they raise stone that high? And why, sometimes, did it come down?
shots.visual_purpose: A short title, then the two questions asked over Beauvais's section: its high vault, then its flying buttresses [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)]

elements.text: Pulled apart: little or no strength

shots.narration: Start with the stone itself. Stone has little or no strength when it is pulled apart. So a stone building stands largely by keeping its stones pressed together.
shots.visual_purpose: Two stones pulled apart come apart (no strength); then an arch of stones pressed together at every joint stands [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (47 elements)]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: Now put a heavy stone vault on top of two walls. A vault does not simply press down: it also pushes outward, like a bow being bent. That outward push is called thrust, and a document from Amiens shows that builders there were well aware of it.
shots.visual_purpose: The section square on: two walls; the heavy vault is set on them; it presses down, then pushes out (arrows drawn, no magnitudes), the vault lit like a bent bow [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 3 timed steps on romanesque_church_section: fade_out 1, reveal 9, highlight 3]

shots.narration: Romanesque builders had several ways of covering a great church. In the barrel-vaulted type shown here, the heavy vault pushes outward along the whole length of the wall, so walls and supports are thick, stiffened by buttresses. Large openings would weaken the wall that holds the vault, so windows tend to stay small.
shots.visual_purpose: From the section, the camera turns to face the east wall along its length: the wall lights along its whole length, then the buttresses, then the small windows, each as it is named [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 4 timed steps on romanesque_church_section: fade_out 1, highlight 3, highlight 4, highlight 3]

shots.narration: Gothic builders rearranged that system of support. Instead of spreading the push along a thick wall, they directed it toward particular points, and carried it to supports outside. Three tools made that possible: the pointed arch, the rib vault, and the flying buttress.
shots.visual_purpose: The Gothic section square on: the piers light (particular points), then the supports outside; then the three tools light as they are named [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 5 timed steps on gothic_cathedral_section: highlight 2, highlight 4, highlight 6, highlight 10, highlight 8]

elements.text: Conceptual arrows: direction only, not calculated
Illustrations, not the arches of the study (Block, DeJong and Ochsendorf, 2006)

shots.narration: A pointed arch is two arcs of a circle that meet at a point. Over the same span, it can rise higher than a round arch, and a taller arch can push less to the sides. How much less depends on its exact shape, its thickness and the weight it carries. One comparison by MIT engineers, of two other arches, did find that the pointed one pushed less, but that result belongs to those two arches, not to every arch.
shots.visual_purpose: The pointed arch drawn as two arcs meeting at a point; the round arch on the same span; both crowns measured; the push drawn as direction only. No thrust figures: these are not the arches of the study [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (118 elements)]

elements.text: “As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted
“As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted
will stand the rigid arch.”  Robert Hooke, 1675

shots.narration: In 1675, the scientist Robert Hooke summed up an idea about arches in one line. As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch. Hang a chain with a set of weights, and it takes a shape. Turn that shape upside down, and it shows a path the force can follow through an arch carrying the same weights. Change the weights, and the shape changes too.
shots.visual_purpose: A chain is hung and its weights added; then the whole shape turns upside down into an arch; different weights draw a different curve [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (68 elements)]

shots.narration: The pointed arch was not a Gothic invention. It already appears in Burgundy, at the great abbey church of Cluny, whose construction began around 1088, and Columbia University's Amiens project traces it to Islamic sources. At the abbey of Saint-Denis, it was used systematically, together with the other new ideas.
shots.visual_purpose: Short timeline: pointed arches before Gothic [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (60 elements)]

elements.text: Regular crowns help keep complex vaults regular
Wide bay, narrow bay: conceptual diagram

shots.narration: It had a subtler advantage too. Unlike a round arch, a pointed arch can span sections of different widths, called bays, and still reach the same height at its crown. That was a valuable asset for keeping complex vaults regular.
shots.visual_purpose: Round arches drawn over two widths, their crowns at different heights; pointed arches over the same widths, their crowns drawn level [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (141 elements)]

shots.narration: The second tool is the rib vault. In the four-part vault shown here, two ribs cross diagonally over each bay of the building. In this simplified picture, they direct the vault's load toward four points: the piers, or stone pillars, at its corners.
shots.visual_purpose: The church on its floor; one bay is marked, the rest fades but stays while the camera turns under the bay; then the bay stands alone: its piers, the two diagonal ribs one after the other, the stone web; the light runs along the ribs to the four piers [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 12 timed steps on gothic_cathedral_section: highlight 28, ghost 88, fade_out 1, ghost 4, fade_out 49, fade_out 88, reveal 1, reveal 1, highlight 2, reveal 20, highlight 2, highlight 4]

shots.narration: How exactly these vaults stand has been debated for centuries. Engineers following Jacques Heyman assume that the main ribs bring the forces down, and treat the stone between them as a series of parallel arches. So even in that reading, the stone between the ribs carries load.
shots.visual_purpose: Closer on the bay's vault: the ribs light, then every other course of the web (the parallel arches of Heyman's reading), then the whole web: it reads as working stone, never as infill [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 6 timed steps on gothic_cathedral_section: ghost 4, fade_out 89, fade_out 27, highlight 4, highlight 12, highlight 20]

Durham, begun 1093, finished 1133: ribbed vaults, in phases

shots.narration: Ribs were not new either. Durham Cathedral in England, begun in 1093, was completely covered by ribbed vaults by the time it was finished in 1133. Its masons refined them in phases over some forty years. Columbia's project traces ribs to Islamic, Roman and Byzantine sources.
shots.visual_purpose: Durham by its own photograph: the camera climbs from its great piers to its ribbed vault while the timeline below advances to Durham's building years, a band, not one date [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (49 elements)]

shots.narration: This kind of vault changes the job of the wall. With the vault's load directed toward the piers, the wall between them was no longer its main support. It could be thinned, and opened up with wide windows.
shots.visual_purpose: One bay before and after, as it is told: a thick wall with a small window; the load drawn down the piers; the wall pales (no longer the main support), thins, and opens into a wide window [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (96 elements)]

shots.narration: But gathering the thrust does not make it go away. Even reduced, that sideways push remains a threat to the stability of the whole building. It still has to be contained somewhere.
shots.visual_purpose: The cut face of the church, square on: an outward arrow at each springing of the high vault, the high piers it pushes on, and the supports outside still faded; then the camera turns to the east side [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 4 timed steps on gothic_cathedral_section: ghost 4, fade_out 2, fade_out 18, highlight 2]

shots.narration: The answer stands outside the building: the flying buttress. It is a stone arch that picks up the thrust where it leaves the vault, carries it across the aisle roof, and brings it down to a massive pier buttress. Often a pinnacle on top adds weight, to help stabilize the thrust.
shots.visual_purpose: One flying buttress in profile: it returns in full when named, the path follows the narration from the vault over the aisle roof down the pier buttress, and the pinnacle is set on top when it is named [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 10 timed steps on gothic_cathedral_section: ghost 4, fade_out 2, fade_out 18, unghost 1, unghost 1, highlight 1, highlight 1, highlight 1, reveal 1, highlight 1]

elements.text: The picture from Columbia's Amiens project
Rigid supports, standing out from the building

shots.narration: One way to picture it comes from Columbia's Amiens project. It is as if the thick outer wall had been cut into segments, and each segment turned 90 degrees. Those segments become rigid supports, standing out from the building, with exposed arches reaching up to the high vaults.
shots.visual_purpose: The picture itself, in plan: one thick wall is cut into segments, each turns 90 degrees to stand out as a support, and the exposed arches reach from them to the high vault [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (40 elements)]

Chartres today: flying buttresses of the nave
Notre-Dame de Paris: the east end (photograph 2011)

shots.narration: According to France's national library, the first flying buttresses were used to consolidate Romanesque churches that threatened to collapse. It also says that the slanting timber props used while building the vaults were, in effect, made permanent in stone. At Chartres, flying buttresses were part of the original plans. And around the east end of Notre-Dame in Paris, they look almost like a giant external skeleton.
shots.visual_purpose: A schematic section for the two origins the library gives (added outside to consolidate; a timber prop made permanent in stone); then the buildings named, by their own photographs: Chartres, Notre-Dame's east end [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (74 elements)]

shots.narration: Flying buttresses even help carry rainwater off the roof. But above all, builders learned how to exploit them, and cathedrals grew ever taller.
shots.visual_purpose: Half a section: the water's way from the roof along the flying buttress and away from the wall, drawn as it is told; then the system drawn taller, dashed [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (68 elements)]

shots.narration: Why go to all this trouble? Part of the answer is light. At the abbey church of Saint-Denis, Abbot Suger built a new choir between 1140 and 1144. Pointed arches run throughout, every vault is ribbed, and monumental stained glass seems to dissolve the whole structure.
shots.visual_purpose: Saint-Denis, dates and three features (a rights-cleared photograph may replace the card) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (48 elements)]

The new style had to let in as much light as possible

shots.narration: For Suger, light was a sign, a bridge to the divine. France's national library says the new style had to let in as much light as possible.
shots.visual_purpose: Why light mattered [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (4 elements)]

elements.text: Suger's crypt: round arches, groin vaults

shots.narration: How new was all of this? Some historians call Gothic a revolution in the art of building, while others see a creative step rooted in continuity. Suger's own crypt still relies almost entirely on round arches and groin vaults.
shots.visual_purpose: Two readings, side by side; the names stay in small type on the card and are not spoken [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (9 elements)]

elements.text: A geometrical rule: compass and line

shots.narration: So how did they do all this, without modern structural calculations? Master builders used geometrical rules, developed through centuries of trial and error. They scaled up the same proportions for new, larger elements.
shots.visual_purpose: An arch drawn with compass and line; the same proportion drawn again, larger, twice [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (85 elements)]

shots.narration: At Amiens, setting out the site began with ropes pegged to the ground. Squares with perfect right angles controlled the plan, and templates for piers, windows and vaults were designed with straight-edge and compass.
shots.visual_purpose: Pegs driven, ropes stretched between them; a square turned inside the square; a straight edge and a compass arc [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (89 elements)]

elements.text: Drawn full size on the ground
Each cut to a wooden template
Amiens: after a couple of months or so

shots.narration: Arches were usually drawn full size on the ground, then divided into wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs. Each voussoir was cut to a wooden template, and the stones were laid on a rigid wooden frame called centering. The frame came away only once the mortar had set: at Amiens, after a couple of months or so.
shots.visual_purpose: The arch drawn full size, divided into stones; the centering set up; the stones laid on it from both sides to the key; the centering taken away once the mortar has set. A building sequence, schematic [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (56 elements)]

shots.narration: Carpenters built the scaffolding, the formwork for the vaults and the lifting gear. They also tied the upper piers with wood, and later iron, to stop the arches pushing them over.
shots.visual_purpose: Each work of the carpenters drawn as it is named: scaffolding, the formwork under a vault, lifting gear; then a tie between the upper piers, wood then iron, against the arches' push. Schematic, no workers [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (201 elements)]

shots.narration: And there was little room for error. The whole stone skeleton relies on lining up the thrust of each arch with the buttress that supports it.
shots.visual_purpose: Close on the point where the flyer meets the pier [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold gothic_cathedral_section, glowing flying_buttress, pier_buttress from sentence 1; slow push-in (12%)]

shots.narration: All of this took generations of work. The foundation stone of Amiens was laid in 1220, and its main roof was not finished until about 1310.
shots.visual_purpose: Ninety years on one line [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (50 elements)]

shots.narration: Which brings us back to Beauvais. In 1225, a fire damaged the old Romanesque choir, and the bishop decided to rebuild it, inspired by the greatest buildings of his time.
shots.visual_purpose: The real building first, filling the frame: the choir of Beauvais today, then the date [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)]

shots.narration: By the 1250s, the two lower levels of the new choir were finished. Then the bishop apparently decided to go beyond the planned proportions, adding about five meters to the upper windows, and so to the vaults. By 1272, the clergy could use the new choir.
shots.visual_purpose: The choir itself: its three levels marked; the camera moves in on the upper windows when they are said to grow [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (21 elements)]

shots.narration: Its vault rose more than 45 meters, a few meters above Amiens. These were the highest vaults built in the Middle Ages.

elements.text: Vault cells over the choir's straight bays fell

shots.narration: Then, in November 1284, part of the vaults over the choir came down. The architect Viollet-le-Duc, writing centuries later, called it the last limit that the great churches of the 13th century could reach.
shots.visual_purpose: Beauvais's own plan, whole; the camera moves in on the straight bays where vault cells fell, marked; no collapse is shown [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (32 elements)]

Why did the vaults fall? Still debated.
Hypothesis: gusts of wind set the
Their hypothesis: vaults raised against proven
proportions left the upper parts too flexible
ECSMGE 2024: an argument, not a settled result

shots.narration: Why it happened is still debated. Some blame settling masonry that broke the flying buttresses. Others point to gusts of wind setting the buttress system resonating, or to slow settlement of the foundations. A 2024 study found nothing to justify a foundation cause. Its authors argue that raising the vaults, against proven proportions, left the upper parts too flexible.
shots.visual_purpose: One hypothesis at a time on Viollet-le-Duc's section of Beauvais, the camera on the part each names; the 2024 study greys the foundation hypothesis (not supported by that study, not ruled out); their argument last [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (91 elements)]

elements.text: New piers between the old ones (positions schematic)
“Longer to repair the choir than to build it”: Stephen Murray

shots.narration: The repair tells its own story. New piers went up between the old ones, turning three bays into six. The work was not finished until 1340: as the historian Stephen Murray put it, it took longer to repair the choir than to build it.
shots.visual_purpose: The plan, then close on the three straight bays: numbered 1 to 3, the new piers appear, the bays become 1 to 6; then out again for the date [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (33 elements)]

elements.text: Photo: Chris06, CC0, Wikimedia Commons; plan: Viollet-le-Duc, 1856
Beauvais Cathedral today: transept and choir
No nave: no support to the west

shots.narration: In the sixteenth century, work began again, with a new transept, the cross-arm of the building. Then, instead of a nave, the builders raised a lantern tower and spire about 150 meters high, finished in 1569. It rested on four slender piers, and the sources point to a lack of support on the west side, where the nave had not been built. In 1573, just four years after it was finished, the tower came down. The great Gothic nave was never built.
shots.visual_purpose: The building today, then its plan: the crossing and its four piers, then the west side where no nave stands; back to the photograph; the timeline moves on to each date. The fall is told, not shown [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (82 elements)]

elements.text: Photo: Eusebius, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
Crossing piers: threatening collapse within two centuries
Iron rods linked together, along the nave, tying the crossing pier

shots.narration: Beauvais was not alone. At Amiens, within two centuries, the piers at the crossing, where the arms of the building meet, were threatening collapse. Between 1497 and 1500, an iron chain was installed to stop the movement, and it still runs through the building today.
shots.visual_purpose: Amiens by its own photograph, then its plan, large: the camera moves in on the crossing piers, then out along the nave while the chain's route is drawn [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (25 elements)]

shots.narration: So why do these buildings stand at all? One answer from modern engineers is that the stone's strength is rarely the limit. Stresses in masonry are typically only a fraction of what the stone can bear, and in most cases structures fail through instability, not a lack of strength.

elements.text: Assumed: stones resist no pulling, never slide, never crush
Many lines can fit. One is enough
Supports moved apart: the arch deforms
At the limit, the line touches the stone at five points
Any further, and no line can fit
After Block, DeJong and Ochsendorf, 2006, Fig. 5, recalculated by Ochsendorf's 2002 method. One idealized arch, self-weight only

shots.narration: Picture one idealized arch, and the path of the force through its stones, which engineers call the line of thrust. This analysis assumes that the stones resist no pulling, never slide and never crush. Under those assumptions and a given load, many such lines can fit inside the masonry, and finding one is enough to show the arch can stand. Now move its supports apart, and the arch deforms. Past a certain point, no line can fit inside it, and this idealized arch collapses.
shots.visual_purpose: One arch at rest with several valid lines; the same arch with its supports moved apart, up to the limit. The fall itself is not shown [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (77 elements)]

elements.text: Does not prove a real building safe
Rules of geometry, learned by trial and error

shots.narration: That puts shape and proportion at the center of the question. Unlike some other engineering problems, stability can be scaled, so a small model with the same proportions helps show what proportion does. On its own, that does not show a whole real building is safe: this kind of analysis can miss effects such as local crushing, cracking and sliding. But it helps explain how rules of geometry, learned by trial and error, could carry builders so far.
shots.visual_purpose: One shape at two sizes; what the model shows and what it does not [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)]

shots.narration: So the heights were never impossible. Pointed arches gave builders taller, more adaptable shapes, ribs helped direct the load toward the piers, and flying buttresses carried the thrust outside and down to the ground. The walls in between could open up to glass.
shots.visual_purpose: The section once more: ribs, flyer, buttress and windows lit in turn [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold gothic_cathedral_section, glowing rib, flying_buttress, clerestory_window from sentence 1; slow push-in (8%)]

elements.text: Not a simple story of progress
Saint-Denis: a bright choir over a crypt of older forms

shots.narration: But it is not a simple story of progress. Beauvais needed new piers, Amiens needed an iron chain, and Suger's bright choir rose above a crypt of older forms. Each cathedral was a test in stone, built by people who learned from centuries of trial and error.
